title: Tasting a Bit of California Wine History
summary:
I had the good fortune last week of being invited to the home of a wine collector in San Francisco

The post Tasting a Bit of California Wine History appeared first on Vinography.
content:
I had the good fortune last week of being invited to the home of a wine collector in San Francisco who is obsessed with older California wines. Over a home-cooked meal, he pulled treasure after treasure out of his cellar for his guests to taste blind. While I have had the privilege to taste some California wines dating back to the early 1970s occasionally over the last 20 years, I have never had the opportunity to taste so many well-cellared examples in a single sitting. I wasn’t the only one in the room taking detailed notes on the wines.

Everyone, the collector included, expressed astonishment at how few of these wines were dead or faulty. That’s all the more remarkable for the fact that most of these bottles were purchased in the last 20 years at auction. “When I’m just home drinking by myself, the hit rate on bottles like these is much lower,” admitted our host.

Just to frame the era in which most of these bottles were made, here are a few statistics about the California wine industry circa 1974.

California crushed enough wine grapes in 1974 to make approximately 243.4 million gallons of wine, or around 102 million cases of wine, roughly half of what is produced these days and a third of what California produced at its peak in 2017. Roughly one third of that volume would have been unfortified sweet dessert wine.

In 1975, according to Bob Thompson’s Wine Atlas of California with Oregon and Washington, Napa hosted between 40 and 45 wineries. According to the Sonoma Department of Agriculture, Sonoma hosted around 35 to 40 wineries in 1973.

The five most planted wine grape varieties according to 1972 statistics were, in descending order of volume: Carignane, French Colombard, Zinfandel, Grenache, and Barbera. In total, these grapes made up roughly 44% of California’s winegrape production.

The average price per ton of wine grapes in 1974 was $146, down from $207 the year before. Last year the average price per ton across the entire state was $978 per ton. This year in Napa, Cabernet Sauvignon sold for $8,933 per ton, and Cabernet Franc sold for $11,131 per ton.

A lot of people I know in wine think of the 1970s and early 1980s as the golden age of California winemaking, pointing to the lower alcohol levels, the greater tolerance for pyrazines (thanks in part to both cooler times and much less strict sorting regimens) and a greater tendency to make wines with the expectation that they will be aged.

Most of the time, when people are talking about these older California wines, they’re talking about Cabernet Sauvignon. That tends to be most of what is left in people’s cellars now, in large part because it has tended to age better than most other varieties in California, perhaps with the exception of Petite Sirah, which can sometimes seem quite ageless. Zinfandels from this era can also be quite good, though I think there are fewer bottles out there. Pinot Noir remains rarer, its boom in plantings having come a bit later.

Not everyone loves the taste of old wine, of course, but when they’re good, there’s nothing quite like the combination of complexity and romance you get when a bottle older than yourself seems to have so much to say in the glass.

Tasting Notes

These wines are, by definition, all collector’s items at this point. Where I have been able to find the exact vintage for sale online, I have listed prices and provided links to purchase. If you are considering purchasing older wines, please do have a care for provenance. It makes a huge difference.

1977 Villa Mt. Eden Chardonnay, Napa, California
Medium to dark gold in the glass, this wine smells of candied citrus peel, butterscotch, and dried herbs. In the mouth, butterscotch, candied citrus, honey, dried herbs, and sassafras flavors have a nice sweetish complexion, with softer acidity and a very silky texture. There’s some oxidation here, but it is fairly easy to look past, with the wine still quite alive, as well as a touch of heat in the finish. Decent, but more of a curiosity than something I’d be really excited to drink. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5.

1972 Freemark Abbey Petite Sirah, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, prunes, chocolate, and a hint of molasses. In the mouth, rich dark cherry and cola flavors mix with chocolate, prunes, and a touch of chopped herbs. Lightly grippy tannins are still buffing the edges of the mouth, and there’s definitely still great acidity and length here. Honestly quite tasty and complex, with lovely dark tones that suggest the nooks and crannies of a Victorian library.12.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5.

1979 Niebaum Coppola “Rubicon” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark ruby in the glass with, remarkably, some hints of garnet still in it, this wine smells of chopped herbs, soy sauce, cola, and prunes. In the mouth, prunes, molasses, stewed black cherries, and fleecy tannins still linger thick on the palate. Licorice and hoisin linger in the finish. Decent acidity, but feeling slightly tired. Labeled as table wine (required to be under 14% alcohol), so no alcohol is given on the label. Score: between 8.5 and 9.

1977 Keenan Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon, Spring Mountain District, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of minty black cherry, molasses, and licorice. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherry, sawdust, dried herbs, licorice, and hoisin. Very good acidity remains in this wine, and it offers distinct pleasure and the sort of mountainside freshness that has made me a longtime fan of early vintage Keenan wines. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $138. click to buy.

1976 Caymus Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark blood red in the glass, with a fine haze of sediment, this wine smells of minty cherry and chopped herbs. In the mouth, wonderfully bright cherry, road dust, and minty herbal notes have great freshness and acidity. Very coniferous in quality with powdery tannins. This is simply a delicious wine and a reminder why Caymus became so popular. This wine, of course, was made when the winery could still be considered an artisan production. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $415. click to buy.

1962 Charles Krug Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Medium blood red in the glass, this wine smells of redwood bark, dusty earth, dried herbs, and dried licorice root with just a hint of something incense-like or smoky. In the mouth, juicy dried cherry, road dust, and dried herb flavors retain a lovely freshness thanks to excellent acidity and the ghostly traces of pyrazines. Tight, fine tannins grip the edges of the palate, and the wine still has quite the finish. I have had more of these wines from the 1970s than any other producer in Napa, but this was my first taste of one from the 1960s. 12% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost:

1962 Charles Krug “Vintage Selection” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark blood red in the glass, this wine smells of meaty cherry and cola, hoisin, and road dust. In the mouth, dusty tannins coat the mouth, as muted flavors of dried herbs and dried cherries mix with road dust, and very good acidity keeps things fresh. Hints of licorice linger in the finish, but this, the reserve/flagship bottling from the 62 vintage, is a muddier, muddled bottle in comparison to the normal Cabernet bottling that preceded it in the tasting. It might have had the fresher-looking label, but it wasn’t nearly as tasty as its scruffier sibling. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5.

1971 Ridge Vineyards “York Creek” Petite Sirah, Spring Mountain District, Napa, California
Very dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of tobacco, hoisin, black cherries, and soy sauce. In the mouth, salty flavors of black cherry, smoked meat, and licorice are wrapped in powdery tannins that give the wine an overall fluffy texture. Notes of licorice and cedar linger in the finish with a hint of molasses sweetness. Very good acidity here, and an overall savory, saline undertone that makes it quite easy to drink. 13.4% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $472. click to buy.

1970 Ridge Vineyards “Jimsomare” Zinfandel, Santa Cruz Mountains, California
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of hoisin and Worcestershire sauce, cola, and prunes. In the mouth, slightly vegetal flavors of stewed cherries and prunes mix with dried herbs, and surprisingly good acidity. Faint gauzy tannins coat the mouth, but this wine is tired and ends up feeling a bit flat on the palate. The wine’s 15.8% alcohol is a bit surprising, as the 1970 vintage wasn’t overly warm. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $. click to buy.

1975 Heitz “Martha’s Vineyard” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass with ruby highlights, this wine smells of black cherries, chopped green herbs, road dust, and a touch of licorice. In the mouth, black cherry, cola, and hoisin flavors are wrapped in powdery, fluffy tannins. The wine offers a lot of herbal freshness with great acidity, and an excellent length on the palate with a positively lovely supple texture. Tasted from magnum, which probably made a good bit of difference. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $1299. click to buy.

1976 Robert Mondavi Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Hazy dark blood red in the glass, this wine smells of red miso, black cherry, and smoked meats. In the mouth, black cherry, chopped herbs, and slightly saline flavors of plum and licorice are surrounded by faint powdery tannins. Excellent acidity and that herbal quality give this wine a positively beautiful freshness. I think this was my favorite bottle of the evening. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5.

1974 Robert Mondavi Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark ruby in the glass with a fine haze of sediment, this wine smells of earth and black cherry. In the mouth, thick, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherry, licorice, faintly salty roasted fig, and dried herbs. There’s a darker earthiness here and a density that I don’t remember from previous tastes of this wine, but at this age there’s no such thing as a “representative” bottle. They’re all unique. This one was pretty good, but not as good as I know it can be, thanks to this being my birth-year wine. 13% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $500. click to buy.

1960 Inglenook Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass with blood red at the rim, this wine smells of Worcestershire sauce, black plums, and black cherries. In the mouth, despite a somewhat tired aroma, the wine is quite fresh and minty, with flavors of black cherry, roasted fig, licorice, and brown sugar wrapped in fine gauzy tannins that add a nice texture but don’t stick to the edges of the mouth. Very good acidity still after 66 years seems something of a marvel. This is the oldest California wine I have had the pleasure of trying, and it was a delight for its age. 12% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $639. click to buy.

1978 Cuvaison Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass, with blood red highlights, this wine smells of cocoa powder, black cherry, mint, and licorice root. In the mouth, powdery, fleecy tannins surround a juicy core of black cherry, stewed plums, and earth. The tannins here are still thick and muscular, but the acidity is quite fresh and herbal. This one seems to have some staying power, and isn’t coasting into its golden years quite yet. Pretty impressive, and a label that suggests nearly perfect storage. 14% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $425. click to buy.

1966 Martin Ray Cabernet Sauvignon, California
Who doesn’t like a little self-aggrandizement from a wine bottle? “A great wine of a superior year” reads the label. A light, hazy blood red in the glass, this wine smells of volatile acidity, redcurrant, and dried herbs. In the mouth, the wine was very sharp, volatile, angular, and shrill, with vinegar and red fruits competing for attention. Sadly not one for the ages, as they say. 13% alcohol. Score: around 7.

1974 Sterling Vineyards “Reserve” Cabernet Sauvignon, California
Very dark ruby in the glass with a faint haze and a hint of blood red at the edge, this wine smells of Worcestershire sauce, black cherries, and roasted figs. In the mouth, bright acidity has a faint angular volatility with flavors of black cherries, sour cherries, herbs, and a touch of licorice. Faint powdery tannins coat the mouth. Still quite fresh, but a little volatile and sweaty. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $495. click to buy.

1974 Stag’s Leap Winery “Cask 23” Cabernet Sauvignon, California
Very dark blood red in the glass, this wine smells of cedar and dried cherries, freshly chopped herbs, and a touch of licorice root. In the mouth, fresh, juicy flavors of dried cherries, chopped green herbs, cola, and a hint of cocoa powder swirl under a throw of powdery tannins. There’s wonderful freshness left in this wine, and quite a bit of pleasure. Perhaps my second favorite wine of the night, and one that made me still feel quite young myself. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $899. click to buy.

title: Coastal Brilliance: Recent Releases from Hirsch Vineyards
summary:
This past July 28th, the wine world mourned the death of pioneering winegrower David Hirsch, who showed the California wine

The post Coastal Brilliance: Recent Releases from Hirsch Vineyards appeared first on Vinography.
content:
This past July 28th, the wine world mourned the death of pioneering winegrower David Hirsch, who showed the California wine industry, and the wider world, that Pinot Noir could be grown brilliantly a mere 3 miles from the chilly Pacific Ocean in the shadow of towering redwoods.

A 2014 tractor accident put the then-70-year-old Hirsch in a wheelchair and hastened his daughter Jasmine’s move into the role of general manager in 2015. She also became the estate’s winemaker in 2019, at which point consulting winemaker Michael Cruse also joined the team. After a long recovery, the elder Hirsch continued to work in the vineyards and winery until shortly before his death this summer.

I’ve been tasting wines made from Hirsch Vineyard fruit for the last 20 years, and have been lucky enough to own a number of bottles dating back to the early 1990s made by Littorai and Williams-Selyem. The evolution of the winery since the estate launched its own wines in 2002 has been remarkable. What has always been a site capable of conveying a purity of stony power and grit, with its more beguiling charms unlocked only by some time in the bottle, has become a place of much more approachable complexity and subtle differentiation.

To put it bluntly: for years, many Hirsch wines were hard to drink in their youth—somewhat impenetrable and slow to demonstrate their grace. Today, speaking especially of the wines made under the estate’s own label, that is no longer the case. While still offering incredible structure, delineation, nervosity, and stony, herbal minerality, Hirsch wines are more perfumed, more complex, more expressive, and more pleasurable to drink in their youth. They only get better with time in the bottle. Some of this undoubtedly has to do with maturation—of the vines themselves, and of the farming practices and team that cares for them—but there is more afoot.

I’m not willing to give the vines all the credit. Hirsch Vineyards is making better wines than it ever has, and I think it’s mostly Jasmine’s fault.

A Remarkable Place

Hirsch’s 72 planted acres sit within a 1,000-acre property atop a ridgeline at 1,500 feet of elevation with views of the Pacific Ocean. The winemaking project began with a mere 2 acres of Pinot Noir, put into the ground with great difficulty in 1980, two years after Hirsch purchased the abandoned sheep ranch with some idea of joining the back-to-the-land movement. At that time, hardly anyone had dreamed of making wine, let alone Pinot Noir, so close to the Pacific. Today, that small section of the West Sonoma Coast has its own AVA named Fort Ross-Seaview, established in 2012.

Inundated by coastal fog, battered by chilly winds straight off the Pacific, the estate receives an average of 80 inches of rain each winter, and then virtually none all summer, as the sun bakes the scraggly grasses and cover crops brown and crispy.

Just half a mile from the San Andreas Fault (on the east side, safe from that mythical fate of falling into the ocean one day), the estate’s mixed-up, diverse geology and undulating topography have been shaped by the grinding forces at work along that famous fault.

Lovingly described by the Hirsch team as “haphazard,” the soils of the estate are indeed a dizzying array of sedimentary (ranging from sand to iron-rich sandstone to shale) and metamorphic (schists and serpentines) layered over deeper basaltic formations that underlie parts of the Coast Range.

Today the estate has been carefully replanted and divided into 67 discrete farming blocks which are used to assemble the estate’s portfolio of Pinot Noirs, a rosé, and a Chardonnay. Some wines are expressions of individual blocks, some are assembled from contiguous parcels, and others represent blends of many or even all the estate’s plantings.

The vineyards have been cultivated using biodynamic principles since 2011 by a vineyard team led by Everardo Robledo, who lives on site and has been managing the vineyards for more than 30 years.

An Intuitive Cellar

As you might expect from a property that has been taking a biodynamic approach for 15 years, winemaking at Hirsch remains fairly simple and low-intervention. After a long cold soak, grapes are fermented in open-top fermenters with ambient yeasts, rarely using whole clusters for Pinot Noir. The site’s exposure and thin soils result in tiny clusters of concentrated grapes with thick skins, all of which means plenty of tannic structure without getting the stems involved. The Chardonnay is pressed as whole clusters to barrel for fermentation with ambient yeasts.

Punchdowns and pumpovers are used gently for extraction of Pinot Noir, and then the red wines are pressed off to barrel using a basket press. All wines go through natural malolactic conversion in their own time. Most wines spend between 11 and 18 months in mostly used oak (30% new for Pinot Noir, 20-25% new for Chardonnay) before being bottled. Hirsch prefers to bottle-age wines anywhere from 12 to 24 months before putting them on sale.

In 2020, the winery produced its first rosé, a wine that Jasmine and her father had talked about making for years. While most rosé producers aim for freshness in the form of short fermentations and a quick release to the market, Hirsch takes a very different approach, making their rosé much more like their Chardonnay.

The fruit is picked just a few days before it would be picked for their normal Pinot Noir, then partially destemmed and pressed into 30% new French oak barrels for fermentation. It ages for 10 months on the lees in barrel and then another 10 to 12 months in bottle before release, yielding a darker, extremely complex and ageworthy rosé that rewards contemplation. A porch pounder this is not. It is savory and tannic, carrying herbal and nutty tones, and doesn’t try to hide its oak influence.

The introduction of the estate’s rosé and the evolution of its wines are part and parcel of what I see as a progression in the estate’s expression of its unique site, guided by an increasingly sensitive mind and hand.

Since taking over winemaking in 2019, Jasmine Hirsch has been working both in the vineyard and in the cellar to achieve more balance between the site’s tannin expression and what she calls “fruit concentration” in the wine. Anywhere else in Northern California, the idea of driving towards more fruit concentration in Pinot Noir might give me pause. But on the windswept ridgetops of the far West Sonoma Coast where sometimes it’s hard to grow Pinot Noir that tops 12% in alcohol, the idea of fruit concentration is a little less scary.

The work that Jasmine and team have been doing in the vineyard (replanting, adjusting row orientations, managing soil health) and in the cellar (gentler infusion than hard extraction, softer pressings) has changed the shape of the wines on the palate. They are more inviting, more nuanced, and ultimately more expressive and pleasurable.

I’m incredibly impressed with the trajectory of Hirsch wines, and can’t wait to see what the site and its winemaker are capable of in the coming decades. David Hirsch spent decades proving that his ridgetop could make great wine. His daughter is now showing us just how great they can be.

Tasting Notes

2024 Hirsch Vineyards Chardonnay, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon zest, lemon oil, and a hint of something deliciously smoky. In the mouth, saline flavors of lemon peel, lemon curd, and white flowers have an admirable seamlessness and breadth, while notes of white flowers and a hint of dried herbs add dimension over a stony foundation. The acidity here is delicate and filigreed, just strong enough to keep the wine from feeling flat. The dried herbs linger in the finish. Biodynamically grown fruit was whole-cluster pressed and fermented in French and Eastern European oak with ambient yeasts and no stirring. Aged for 11 months on the lees in 25% new oak and then racked to stainless steel for one month before bottling. 13.5% alcohol. 1200 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $96. click to buy.

2024 Hirsch Vineyards Rosé of Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink in the glass, this wine smells of berries, crushed nuts, and dried flowers. In the mouth, strawberry and raspberry flavors are silky smooth and shot through with dried herbs, crushed nuts, and a hint of vanilla. A faint tannic texture hangs at the edges of perception as citrus peel, sweet berries, and cream linger in the finish. Very good acidity. This is a rosé built for the long haul. Biodynamically grown fruit was destemmed and macerated overnight, then pressed. Fermented in 32% new oak with ambient yeasts and no stirring. Aged 10 months post-fermentation in the same barrels. Then aged 10 more months in bottle before release. 13.5% alcohol. 400 cases made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $45. click to buy.

2023 Hirsch Vineyards “Raschen Ridge” Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet earth, cherries, herbs, and wet pavement. title: Introducing the Old Vine Registry Seal
summary:
I can’t tell you how many times I’ve picked up a bottle of wine that had the words “old vines,”

The post Introducing the Old Vine Registry Seal appeared first on Vinography.
content:
I can’t tell you how many times I’ve picked up a bottle of wine that had the words “old vines,” “vieilles vignes,” or “vigna vecchia” on the label and turned it around to find absolutely no further information about the vineyard that produced it. Were the vines 40 years old or 140? Did this come from one old vineyard or several? Those two words seem to be doing an awful lot of work while, at the same time, meaning almost nothing.

With the exception of a few regions in Spain (Priorat, Rioja, Ribera del Duero) and in Greece, the term “old vines” isn’t officially regulated or defined anywhere. Producers are free to use it however they like, regardless of actual vine age. And the reverse happens just as often: plenty of wines genuinely made from old vines never mention it at all, either because producers can’t be bothered, or because all of their vines are old and it doesn’t feel worth saying on every bottle.

That problem, multiplied by the hundreds of thousands around the world, is a big part of why the Old Vine Registry exists, and today I’m extremely proud to announce the next step in that project: the launch of the Old Vine Registry Seal. The OVR Seal is a program that allows producers, retailers, and importers to showcase wines made from the vineyards cataloged in the Old Vine Registry.

Wines made from old vines are special. They are different. They are less common. And consumers might appreciate that fact a bit more if they only had a way of consistently recognizing wines that were made from old vineyards around the world.

That’s what we’ve designed the OVR Seal to do. It clearly communicates that a wine comes from a registered vineyard, as well as the age category of that vineyard: 35+, 50+, 75+, 100+, and 150+ years old.

The seal, designed in several formats, is intended primarily for use on wine labels, but it can also appear on tech sheets, marketing materials, websites, e-commerce pages, and even vineyard signs, provided it remains associated with a specific registered vineyard, or a specific wine made from a registered vineyard.

It’s taken several months of hard work to pull this program together, with the help of stakeholders from several countries providing input into the early design drafts of the seal as well as the structure and terms of the program.

Meet the Launch Partners

The seal launches today with 11 initial launch partners—producers from 7 different countries—who were especially keen to be among the first to adopt the OVR Seal. They are:

  • AYA Estate – a beautiful Relais & Châteaux property in the Melnik region of Bulgaria with several plots of 51-year-old Cabernet Franc vines. Their 2024 Melnik, produced by Seewines Spirit and about to be released, will be the first commercially available bottle in the world bearing the OVR seal.
  • Bedrock Wine Co. – this Sonoma producer is one of the world’s premier stewards of old vineyards and a thought leader on old-vine wines and viticulture. Owner Morgan Twain-Peterson MW has written a very thoughtful article on why he is adopting the seal. Bedrock has a number of vineyards in the Old Vine Registry, including their eponymous Bedrock Vineyard, planted in 1888. The OVR Seal will appear on their 2026 wines, which will be released beginning in 2027.
  • Bodega Ciclo Andino – this boutique producer in Mendoza, Argentina, farms 18 acres of own-rooted Malbec vines planted in 1920. They will be using the OVR Seal on the soon-to-be-released 2024 vintage of their “Mas de Cien” Reserve Malbec.
  • Garage Wine Company – another globally recognized champion of old-vine wines and viticulture, founder Derek Mossman Knapp collaborates with farmers of several ancient vineyards in the Maule region of Chile, such as Nivaldo Morales and his 1900-planted Sauzal Vineyard. All of the Garage wines except those from Maipo will soon feature the OVR seal.
  • Methymnaeos Organic Vineyards – one of the pioneers of modern viticulture on the Greek island of Lesvos, Methymnaeos farms the oldest documented commercial planting on the island. Owner and winemaker Yannis Lambrou will use the OVR Seal on the upcoming releases of his 2023 and 2024 wines beginning in June of 2027.
  • Plaimont – this cooperative in the Gascony region of France has revitalized one of France’s oldest vineyards, the famous 1820-planted Pédebernarde vineyard, and farms many acres of old vineyards in Gascony and the Pyrenean foothills. Several of their wines will carry the OVR seal, but the first two to market will be their La Madeleine de Saint Mont and their Série XT Colombard Vieilles Vignes, both to be released in 2027.
  • Seghesio Family Vineyards – one of the most famous names in California Zinfandel, Seghesio farms several ancient vineyards, including their well-known Chianti Station vineyard planted in 1910. Seghesio will be using the OVR Seal on future bottlings of their Montafi Ranch Red Blend, Seghesio Home Ranch Zinfandel, and Chianti Station Sangiovese Blend.
  • Sown Estate – a newer, family-run property in Napa, Sown Estate farms a spectacular 35-year-old hillside vineyard at 1,100 feet of elevation on the slopes of Mount George in Napa above the Coombsville AVA. Their estate wines will feature the OVR Seal when they are next labeled and bottled.
  • Tenuta Santa Maria di Gaetano Bertani – The Bertani family has been making wine in the Veneto region since at least 1567. Among their many vineyard holdings is the 1965-planted Lepiga Vineyard. Tenuta Santa Maria will be featuring the OVR Seal on their 2026 Lepiga Soave, which will be released in 2027.
  • Versado Wine – This tiny producer in the Lujan de Cuyo region of Mendoza in Argentina farms 7.4 acres of own-rooted Malbec planted in 1920. Their 2020 Centenary Vines Malbec, to be released in March of 2027, will carry the OVR Seal.
  • Wooldridge Creek Winery – located in Oregon’s Applegate Valley, this family-run estate farms a large vineyard site planted in the late 1970s and early 1980s. They produce an array of wines that will soon bear the OVR Seal.

Why This Matters

The Old Vine Registry’s mission has three pillars: Identify, Value, and Preserve. The registry exists first to identify and catalog old vineyards around the world for the simple reason that you can’t preserve what you don’t know about. Secondly, the stories of these vineyards, the people who farm them, and the wines they make need to be documented and told. Only then will people understand the value of these vineyards and be willing to pay for the wines they produce. If we can get people to buy the wines, then the vineyards will continue to have economic value for those who farm them, and we can begin the conversation around preserving them. We don’t preserve what we don’t value.

As the largest and most authoritative database of 35+ year-old vineyards around the world, the Old Vine Registry has made great progress on the identification piece of that mission. We’ve come a long way from an 1800-line spreadsheet in just three years, but there’s plenty more work ahead. The OVR Seal represents the next step towards fulfilling that mission. By giving wine producers, importers, and retailers the ability to clearly identify wines made from registered vineyards, we’re hoping to move the old-vine conversation down to the level of the shelf or the wine list, where it actually reaches wine drinkers.

The hope is that the OVR Seal can play a part in helping to create a viable commercial category for old-vine wines. It’s not hard to imagine a day when you could walk into a wine shop and find a section dedicated to old-vine wines, or filter an e-commerce site for them. Restaurants could carve out a section of their wine list, or just put an icon next to old-vine bottles. Importers could let buyers sort and filter their portfolios the same way. When such options become a reality, we will have moved the conversation about old vines and their value to center stage, where it belongs.

If you happen to be a wine producer with a qualifying vineyard, you can submit your vineyard to the Old Vine Registry for free, and once it’s in the database, you can register to use the OVR seal.

If you’re a wine lover, the easiest place to start engaging with old vineyards is to pull an old-vine bottle off the shelf and see whether it’s already in the Registry. If it’s not, you can submit it yourself, or reach out to the producer and encourage them to do so.

So the next time one of us turns around a bottle looking for an answer, we can find one.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 9/20/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 9/20/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep, asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week I received a few bottles from Whitehall Lane in Napa. Their Sauvignon Blanc is a classic representation of the form that delivers bright tropical flavors while being very easy to drink. I wasn’t aware that they also made Pinot Noir, which is decent, but I suppose there’s a benefit to offering a little variation to your customers when you’re smack-dab in the middle of Napa Valley. Their Cabernet Sauvignon from the 2022 vintage offers a lot of ripe fruit qualities that are perhaps a consequence of the warm vintage, and may make the wine slightly less ageworthy than either the 2021 or 2023 vintages.

When it comes to Portuguese fortified wines, everyone knows Port, and some people know Madeira is also from Portugal, but there are a number of other fortified wines produced in the country that would be much more famous were they not overshadowed by the leviathan that is Port (and their historical occupation of some of Portugal’s most attractive real estate). In fact, in the 19th century, the light amber fortified wines of Carcavelos were just as famous as Port. But the region sits on the coast east of Lisbon and over the course of the next 150 years, urban expansion and seaside tourism all but wiped out the vineyards there. Still, a bit of viticulture (a mere 22 hectares) clings to life, from which Villa Oeiras (for the longest time, the only game in town) makes a traditional fortified sweet white wine that brims with acidity and caramelized flavors.

Moscatel de Setubal enjoys slightly less threatened status as a wine, in large part thanks to the efforts of José Maria da Fonseca, who is credited with not only pioneering the style of the region’s fortified wines, but also keeping the production of these wines relatively robust since the early 1800s. The wines take their name from the Setubal Peninsula, south of Lisbon, where both dry and sweet wines are produced, but where sweet fortified wines made from Muscat have long been the most famous. Roughly 330 hectares remain dedicated to Moscatel de Setubal production, with José Maria da Fonseca still the dominant regional force, along with half a dozen other smaller wineries. The 20-year-old bottling from Fonseca I’m recommending this week is a great demonstration of why these wines were so well-regarded historically. It’s beautiful and manages to be refreshing despite its sweetness. Interest in the wines (as with most fortified wines) has been dropping in recent years, so drinking a bottle can help support this storied appellation, which, in 1907, was the second demarcated wine region in Portugal after the Dão.

One of the things I love about rosé wine is the sheer breadth and variety of styles you can find in the category, from the palest pinks to wines that approach the hues you expect from red wines. The Rosa di Lupo rosé from COS Winery in the Vittoria region of Sicily sits somewhere in the middle, offering a slightly darker color and some tannic grip in addition to all the wonderful freshness and saline brightness that I love in a good rosé. Made from Nero d’Avola, the wine is a wonderful expression of the effortlessly delicious style of COS wines.

To finish up this week, I received three single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignons from Nickel and Nickel winery in Napa, which is part of the Far Niente empire. All three are from the 2023 vintage, and each demonstrates the impressive quality of that year. As usual, these bottlings are reliably delicious and very well made, rewarding anyone who’s willing to spend $100 on a Cabernet with all the grace and power you’d typically look for in Napa Cabernet without getting close to being over-the-top.

Notes on all these wines below.

Tasting Notes

2025 Whitehall Lane Sauvignon Blanc, Rutherford, Napa, California
Palest straw in color, this wine smells of golden apples, passionfruit, and lemon zest. In the mouth, bright passionfruit and golden apple flavors have a very good level of acidity and a faint floral sweetness that lingers in the finish. 13.9% alcohol. Closed with a screwcap. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $30. click to buy.

MV Villa Oeiras “15 Year Old” Vinho Generoso, Carcavelos, Lisboa, Portugal
Light amber in the glass, this wine smells of acetone, candied citrus peel, and caramel. In the mouth, moderate to very sweet flavors of vanilla caramel, butterscotch, candied citrus, and hints of cafe-au-lait linger for minutes in the finish. Great acidity. A blend of Arinto, Flego Dourado, Ratinho. Composed of barrel-aged vintages averaging 15 years of age. Fortified to 18.5% alcohol. 104 g/L residual sugar. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $52. click to buy.

MV José Maria da Fonseca Vinhos “Alambre 20 Year-Old” Moscatel de Setubal, Península de Setúbal, Portugal
Medium amber in color, this wine smells of acetone, caramel, brown sugar, vanilla, and maple sugar. In the mouth, flavors of vanilla, caramel, butterscotch, candied orange, and a hint of baking spice linger for minutes on the palate. Fresh acidity is bright enough to give an almost minty quality. Very sweet. Aged in used wood, and made from a blend of vintages ranging from 1911 to 2006. The 20-year designation is the minimum age of any wine to be used in the blend. Fortified to 17.1% alcohol. 157.2 g/L residual sugar. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $80. click to buy.

2025 COS “Rosa di Lupo” Rosato of Nero d’Avola, Sicily, Italy
Pale to light ruby in the glass, this wine smells of stony berries and herbs. In the mouth, a faint tannic grip adds texture to saline flavors of sour cherry, citrus peel, rosehips, and rhubarb. Juicy and bright with excellent acidity, this wine has a lovely freshness and snappiness that make it a joy to drink. 11.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $28. click to buy.

2023 Whitehall Lane “Sonoma Stage Vineyard” Pinot Noir, Petaluma Gap, Sonoma, California
Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of oak and cherries, anise, and dried herbs. In the mouth, gauzy tannins wrap around a core of cherry and raspberry flavors shot through with cola and cedar notes. Dried herbs linger a bit in the finish. Decent acidity. 13.9% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $??.

2022 Whitehall Lane Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, tobacco, a hint of black olives, and a touch of grapey-ness. In the mouth, supple, fleecy tannins surround a core of black cherry, cola, and that Concord-grape note that showed up in the nose and lingers in the finish. Very good acidity. 14.7% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $56. click to buy.

2023 Nickel & Nickel “John C. Sullenger Vineyard” Cabernet Sauvignon, Oakville, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass with purple highlights, this wine smells of black cherries, cassis, and a hint of cola. In the mouth, muscular, fleecy tannins surround a core of black cherry, blackberry, and black currant flavors shot through with dried herbs and a touch of milk chocolate. Excellent acidity. 14.8% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $107. click to buy.

2023 Nickel & Nickel “DeCarle Block” Cabernet Sauvignon, Rutherford, Napa, California
Very dark garnet with purple highlights, this wine smells of black cherries, blackberries, and cola. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherry and blackberry fruit shot through with vanilla and the nutty espresso notes of oak that linger in the finish. The tannins stiffen with time, but excellent acidity keeps things fresh. 14.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $117. click to buy.

2023 Nickel & Nickel “Fog Break Vineyard” Cabernet Sauvignon, Atlas Peak, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass with purple highlights, this wine smells of black cherries and cassis. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherries, black plums, cola nut, and cassis as hints of flowers emerge in the finish. The tannins stiffen a bit with time, and excellent acidity keeps things fresh and vibrant on the palate. Very pretty and delicious. 14.8% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $115. click to buy.

title: Tasting a Bit of California Wine History
summary:
I had the good fortune last week of being invited to the home of a wine collector in San Francisco

The post Tasting a Bit of California Wine History appeared first on Vinography.
content:
I had the good fortune last week of being invited to the home of a wine collector in San Francisco who is obsessed with older California wines. Over a home-cooked meal, he pulled treasure after treasure out of his cellar for his guests to taste blind. While I have had the privilege to taste some California wines dating back to the early 1970s occasionally over the last 20 years, I have never had the opportunity to taste so many well-cellared examples in a single sitting. I wasn’t the only one in the room taking detailed notes on the wines.

Everyone, the collector included, expressed astonishment at how few of these wines were dead or faulty. That’s all the more remarkable for the fact that most of these bottles were purchased in the last 20 years at auction. “When I’m just home drinking by myself, the hit rate on bottles like these is much lower,” admitted our host.

Just to frame the era in which most of these bottles were made, here are a few statistics about the California wine industry circa 1974.

California crushed enough wine grapes in 1974 to make approximately 243.4 million gallons of wine, or around 102 million cases of wine, roughly half of what is produced these days and a third of what California produced at its peak in 2017. Roughly one third of that volume would have been unfortified sweet dessert wine.

In 1975, according to Bob Thompson’s Wine Atlas of California with Oregon and Washington, Napa hosted between 40 and 45 wineries. According to the Sonoma Department of Agriculture, Sonoma hosted around 35 to 40 wineries in 1973.

The five most planted wine grape varieties according to 1972 statistics were, in descending order of volume: Carignane, French Colombard, Zinfandel, Grenache, and Barbera. In total, these grapes made up roughly 44% of California’s winegrape production.

The average price per ton of wine grapes in 1974 was $146, down from $207 the year before. Last year the average price per ton across the entire state was $978 per ton. This year in Napa, Cabernet Sauvignon sold for $8,933 per ton, and Cabernet Franc sold for $11,131 per ton.

A lot of people I know in wine think of the 1970s and early 1980s as the golden age of California winemaking, pointing to the lower alcohol levels, the greater tolerance for pyrazines (thanks in part to both cooler times and much less strict sorting regimens) and a greater tendency to make wines with the expectation that they will be aged.

Most of the time, when people are talking about these older California wines, they’re talking about Cabernet Sauvignon. That tends to be most of what is left in people’s cellars now, in large part because it has tended to age better than most other varieties in California, perhaps with the exception of Petite Sirah, which can sometimes seem quite ageless. Zinfandels from this era can also be quite good, though I think there are fewer bottles out there. Pinot Noir remains rarer, its boom in plantings having come a bit later.

Not everyone loves the taste of old wine, of course, but when they’re good, there’s nothing quite like the combination of complexity and romance you get when a bottle older than yourself seems to have so much to say in the glass.

Tasting Notes

These wines are, by definition, all collector’s items at this point. Where I have been able to find the exact vintage for sale online, I have listed prices and provided links to purchase. If you are considering purchasing older wines, please do have a care for provenance. It makes a huge difference.

1977 Villa Mt. Eden Chardonnay, Napa, California
Medium to dark gold in the glass, this wine smells of candied citrus peel, butterscotch, and dried herbs. In the mouth, butterscotch, candied citrus, honey, dried herbs, and sassafras flavors have a nice sweetish complexion, with softer acidity and a very silky texture. There’s some oxidation here, but it is fairly easy to look past, with the wine still quite alive, as well as a touch of heat in the finish. Decent, but more of a curiosity than something I’d be really excited to drink. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5.

1972 Freemark Abbey Petite Sirah, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, prunes, chocolate, and a hint of molasses. In the mouth, rich dark cherry and cola flavors mix with chocolate, prunes, and a touch of chopped herbs. Lightly grippy tannins are still buffing the edges of the mouth, and there’s definitely still great acidity and length here. Honestly quite tasty and complex, with lovely dark tones that suggest the nooks and crannies of a Victorian library.12.5% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5.

1979 Niebaum Coppola “Rubicon” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark ruby in the glass with, remarkably, some hints of garnet still in it, this wine smells of chopped herbs, soy sauce, cola, and prunes. In the mouth, prunes, molasses, stewed black cherries, and fleecy tannins still linger thick on the palate. Licorice and hoisin linger in the finish. Decent acidity, but feeling slightly tired. Labeled as table wine (required to be under 14% alcohol), so no alcohol is given on the label. Score: between 8.5 and 9.

1977 Keenan Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon, Spring Mountain District, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of minty black cherry, molasses, and licorice. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherry, sawdust, dried herbs, licorice, and hoisin. Very good acidity remains in this wine, and it offers distinct pleasure and the sort of mountainside freshness that has made me a longtime fan of early vintage Keenan wines. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $138. click to buy.

1976 Caymus Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark blood red in the glass, with a fine haze of sediment, this wine smells of minty cherry and chopped herbs. In the mouth, wonderfully bright cherry, road dust, and minty herbal notes have great freshness and acidity. Very coniferous in quality with powdery tannins. This is simply a delicious wine and a reminder why Caymus became so popular. This wine, of course, was made when the winery could still be considered an artisan production. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $415. click to buy.

1962 Charles Krug Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Medium blood red in the glass, this wine smells of redwood bark, dusty earth, dried herbs, and dried licorice root with just a hint of something incense-like or smoky. In the mouth, juicy dried cherry, road dust, and dried herb flavors retain a lovely freshness thanks to excellent acidity and the ghostly traces of pyrazines. Tight, fine tannins grip the edges of the palate, and the wine still has quite the finish. I have had more of these wines from the 1970s than any other producer in Napa, but this was my first taste of one from the 1960s. 12% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost:

1962 Charles Krug “Vintage Selection” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark blood red in the glass, this wine smells of meaty cherry and cola, hoisin, and road dust. In the mouth, dusty tannins coat the mouth, as muted flavors of dried herbs and dried cherries mix with road dust, and very good acidity keeps things fresh. Hints of licorice linger in the finish, but this, the reserve/flagship bottling from the 62 vintage, is a muddier, muddled bottle in comparison to the normal Cabernet bottling that preceded it in the tasting. It might have had the fresher-looking label, but it wasn’t nearly as tasty as its scruffier sibling. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5.

1971 Ridge Vineyards “York Creek” Petite Sirah, Spring Mountain District, Napa, California
Very dark ruby in the glass, this wine smells of tobacco, hoisin, black cherries, and soy sauce. In the mouth, salty flavors of black cherry, smoked meat, and licorice are wrapped in powdery tannins that give the wine an overall fluffy texture. Notes of licorice and cedar linger in the finish with a hint of molasses sweetness. Very good acidity here, and an overall savory, saline undertone that makes it quite easy to drink. 13.4% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $472. click to buy.

1970 Ridge Vineyards “Jimsomare” Zinfandel, Santa Cruz Mountains, California
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of hoisin and Worcestershire sauce, cola, and prunes. In the mouth, slightly vegetal flavors of stewed cherries and prunes mix with dried herbs, and surprisingly good acidity. Faint gauzy tannins coat the mouth, but this wine is tired and ends up feeling a bit flat on the palate. The wine’s 15.8% alcohol is a bit surprising, as the 1970 vintage wasn’t overly warm. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $. click to buy.

1975 Heitz “Martha’s Vineyard” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass with ruby highlights, this wine smells of black cherries, chopped green herbs, road dust, and a touch of licorice. In the mouth, black cherry, cola, and hoisin flavors are wrapped in powdery, fluffy tannins. The wine offers a lot of herbal freshness with great acidity, and an excellent length on the palate with a positively lovely supple texture. Tasted from magnum, which probably made a good bit of difference. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $1299. click to buy.

1976 Robert Mondavi Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Hazy dark blood red in the glass, this wine smells of red miso, black cherry, and smoked meats. In the mouth, black cherry, chopped herbs, and slightly saline flavors of plum and licorice are surrounded by faint powdery tannins. Excellent acidity and that herbal quality give this wine a positively beautiful freshness. I think this was my favorite bottle of the evening. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5.

1974 Robert Mondavi Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Very dark ruby in the glass with a fine haze of sediment, this wine smells of earth and black cherry. In the mouth, thick, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherry, licorice, faintly salty roasted fig, and dried herbs. There’s a darker earthiness here and a density that I don’t remember from previous tastes of this wine, but at this age there’s no such thing as a “representative” bottle. They’re all unique. This one was pretty good, but not as good as I know it can be, thanks to this being my birth-year wine. 13% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $500. click to buy.

1960 Inglenook Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass with blood red at the rim, this wine smells of Worcestershire sauce, black plums, and black cherries. In the mouth, despite a somewhat tired aroma, the wine is quite fresh and minty, with flavors of black cherry, roasted fig, licorice, and brown sugar wrapped in fine gauzy tannins that add a nice texture but don’t stick to the edges of the mouth. Very good acidity still after 66 years seems something of a marvel. This is the oldest California wine I have had the pleasure of trying, and it was a delight for its age. 12% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $639. click to buy.

1978 Cuvaison Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark ruby in the glass, with blood red highlights, this wine smells of cocoa powder, black cherry, mint, and licorice root. In the mouth, powdery, fleecy tannins surround a juicy core of black cherry, stewed plums, and earth. The tannins here are still thick and muscular, but the acidity is quite fresh and herbal. This one seems to have some staying power, and isn’t coasting into its golden years quite yet. Pretty impressive, and a label that suggests nearly perfect storage. 14% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $425. click to buy.

1966 Martin Ray Cabernet Sauvignon, California
Who doesn’t like a little self-aggrandizement from a wine bottle? “A great wine of a superior year” reads the label. A light, hazy blood red in the glass, this wine smells of volatile acidity, redcurrant, and dried herbs. In the mouth, the wine was very sharp, volatile, angular, and shrill, with vinegar and red fruits competing for attention. Sadly not one for the ages, as they say. 13% alcohol. Score: around 7.

1974 Sterling Vineyards “Reserve” Cabernet Sauvignon, California
Very dark ruby in the glass with a faint haze and a hint of blood red at the edge, this wine smells of Worcestershire sauce, black cherries, and roasted figs. In the mouth, bright acidity has a faint angular volatility with flavors of black cherries, sour cherries, herbs, and a touch of licorice. Faint powdery tannins coat the mouth. Still quite fresh, but a little volatile and sweaty. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $495. click to buy.

1974 Stag’s Leap Winery “Cask 23” Cabernet Sauvignon, California
Very dark blood red in the glass, this wine smells of cedar and dried cherries, freshly chopped herbs, and a touch of licorice root. In the mouth, fresh, juicy flavors of dried cherries, chopped green herbs, cola, and a hint of cocoa powder swirl under a throw of powdery tannins. There’s wonderful freshness left in this wine, and quite a bit of pleasure. Perhaps my second favorite wine of the night, and one that made me still feel quite young myself. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $899. click to buy.

title: Coastal Brilliance: Recent Releases from Hirsch Vineyards
summary:
This past July 28th, the wine world mourned the death of pioneering winegrower David Hirsch, who showed the California wine

The post Coastal Brilliance: Recent Releases from Hirsch Vineyards appeared first on Vinography.
content:
This past July 28th, the wine world mourned the death of pioneering winegrower David Hirsch, who showed the California wine industry, and the wider world, that Pinot Noir could be grown brilliantly a mere 3 miles from the chilly Pacific Ocean in the shadow of towering redwoods.

A 2014 tractor accident put the then-70-year-old Hirsch in a wheelchair and hastened his daughter Jasmine’s move into the role of general manager in 2015. She also became the estate’s winemaker in 2019, at which point consulting winemaker Michael Cruse also joined the team. After a long recovery, the elder Hirsch continued to work in the vineyards and winery until shortly before his death this summer.

I’ve been tasting wines made from Hirsch Vineyard fruit for the last 20 years, and have been lucky enough to own a number of bottles dating back to the early 1990s made by Littorai and Williams-Selyem. The evolution of the winery since the estate launched its own wines in 2002 has been remarkable. What has always been a site capable of conveying a purity of stony power and grit, with its more beguiling charms unlocked only by some time in the bottle, has become a place of much more approachable complexity and subtle differentiation.

To put it bluntly: for years, many Hirsch wines were hard to drink in their youth—somewhat impenetrable and slow to demonstrate their grace. Today, speaking especially of the wines made under the estate’s own label, that is no longer the case. While still offering incredible structure, delineation, nervosity, and stony, herbal minerality, Hirsch wines are more perfumed, more complex, more expressive, and more pleasurable to drink in their youth. They only get better with time in the bottle. Some of this undoubtedly has to do with maturation—of the vines themselves, and of the farming practices and team that cares for them—but there is more afoot.

I’m not willing to give the vines all the credit. Hirsch Vineyards is making better wines than it ever has, and I think it’s mostly Jasmine’s fault.

A Remarkable Place

Hirsch’s 72 planted acres sit within a 1,000-acre property atop a ridgeline at 1,500 feet of elevation with views of the Pacific Ocean. The winemaking project began with a mere 2 acres of Pinot Noir, put into the ground with great difficulty in 1980, two years after Hirsch purchased the abandoned sheep ranch with some idea of joining the back-to-the-land movement. At that time, hardly anyone had dreamed of making wine, let alone Pinot Noir, so close to the Pacific. Today, that small section of the West Sonoma Coast has its own AVA named Fort Ross-Seaview, established in 2012.

Inundated by coastal fog, battered by chilly winds straight off the Pacific, the estate receives an average of 80 inches of rain each winter, and then virtually none all summer, as the sun bakes the scraggly grasses and cover crops brown and crispy.

Just half a mile from the San Andreas Fault (on the east side, safe from that mythical fate of falling into the ocean one day), the estate’s mixed-up, diverse geology and undulating topography have been shaped by the grinding forces at work along that famous fault.

Lovingly described by the Hirsch team as “haphazard,” the soils of the estate are indeed a dizzying array of sedimentary (ranging from sand to iron-rich sandstone to shale) and metamorphic (schists and serpentines) layered over deeper basaltic formations that underlie parts of the Coast Range.

Today the estate has been carefully replanted and divided into 67 discrete farming blocks which are used to assemble the estate’s portfolio of Pinot Noirs, a rosé, and a Chardonnay. Some wines are expressions of individual blocks, some are assembled from contiguous parcels, and others represent blends of many or even all the estate’s plantings.

The vineyards have been cultivated using biodynamic principles since 2011 by a vineyard team led by Everardo Robledo, who lives on site and has been managing the vineyards for more than 30 years.

An Intuitive Cellar

As you might expect from a property that has been taking a biodynamic approach for 15 years, winemaking at Hirsch remains fairly simple and low-intervention. After a long cold soak, grapes are fermented in open-top fermenters with ambient yeasts, rarely using whole clusters for Pinot Noir. The site’s exposure and thin soils result in tiny clusters of concentrated grapes with thick skins, all of which means plenty of tannic structure without getting the stems involved. The Chardonnay is pressed as whole clusters to barrel for fermentation with ambient yeasts.

Punchdowns and pumpovers are used gently for extraction of Pinot Noir, and then the red wines are pressed off to barrel using a basket press. All wines go through natural malolactic conversion in their own time. Most wines spend between 11 and 18 months in mostly used oak (30% new for Pinot Noir, 20-25% new for Chardonnay) before being bottled. Hirsch prefers to bottle-age wines anywhere from 12 to 24 months before putting them on sale.

In 2020, the winery produced its first rosé, a wine that Jasmine and her father had talked about making for years. While most rosé producers aim for freshness in the form of short fermentations and a quick release to the market, Hirsch takes a very different approach, making their rosé much more like their Chardonnay.

The fruit is picked just a few days before it would be picked for their normal Pinot Noir, then partially destemmed and pressed into 30% new French oak barrels for fermentation. It ages for 10 months on the lees in barrel and then another 10 to 12 months in bottle before release, yielding a darker, extremely complex and ageworthy rosé that rewards contemplation. A porch pounder this is not. It is savory and tannic, carrying herbal and nutty tones, and doesn’t try to hide its oak influence.

The introduction of the estate’s rosé and the evolution of its wines are part and parcel of what I see as a progression in the estate’s expression of its unique site, guided by an increasingly sensitive mind and hand.

Since taking over winemaking in 2019, Jasmine Hirsch has been working both in the vineyard and in the cellar to achieve more balance between the site’s tannin expression and what she calls “fruit concentration” in the wine. Anywhere else in Northern California, the idea of driving towards more fruit concentration in Pinot Noir might give me pause. But on the windswept ridgetops of the far West Sonoma Coast where sometimes it’s hard to grow Pinot Noir that tops 12% in alcohol, the idea of fruit concentration is a little less scary.

The work that Jasmine and team have been doing in the vineyard (replanting, adjusting row orientations, managing soil health) and in the cellar (gentler infusion than hard extraction, softer pressings) has changed the shape of the wines on the palate. They are more inviting, more nuanced, and ultimately more expressive and pleasurable.

I’m incredibly impressed with the trajectory of Hirsch wines, and can’t wait to see what the site and its winemaker are capable of in the coming decades. David Hirsch spent decades proving that his ridgetop could make great wine. His daughter is now showing us just how great they can be.

Tasting Notes

2024 Hirsch Vineyards Chardonnay, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon zest, lemon oil, and a hint of something deliciously smoky. In the mouth, saline flavors of lemon peel, lemon curd, and white flowers have an admirable seamlessness and breadth, while notes of white flowers and a hint of dried herbs add dimension over a stony foundation. The acidity here is delicate and filigreed, just strong enough to keep the wine from feeling flat. The dried herbs linger in the finish. Biodynamically grown fruit was whole-cluster pressed and fermented in French and Eastern European oak with ambient yeasts and no stirring. Aged for 11 months on the lees in 25% new oak and then racked to stainless steel for one month before bottling. 13.5% alcohol. 1200 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $96. click to buy.

2024 Hirsch Vineyards Rosé of Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light coppery pink in the glass, this wine smells of berries, crushed nuts, and dried flowers. In the mouth, strawberry and raspberry flavors are silky smooth and shot through with dried herbs, crushed nuts, and a hint of vanilla. A faint tannic texture hangs at the edges of perception as citrus peel, sweet berries, and cream linger in the finish. Very good acidity. This is a rosé built for the long haul. Biodynamically grown fruit was destemmed and macerated overnight, then pressed. Fermented in 32% new oak with ambient yeasts and no stirring. Aged 10 months post-fermentation in the same barrels. Then aged 10 more months in bottle before release. 13.5% alcohol. 400 cases made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $45. click to buy.

2023 Hirsch Vineyards “Raschen Ridge” Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of wet earth, cherries, herbs, and wet pavement. In the mouth, vibrant flavors of raspberry and cherry fruit are wrapped in fine-grained, very stony tannins that stiffen with musculature as sweet oak, and raspberry pastilles linger in the finish along with chopped herbs and flowers. Excellent acidity. A broad-shouldered wine with cut and electricity. Biodynamically grown fruit was destemmed, cold-soaked, and fermented in open-top fermenters with ambient yeasts with a combination of pumpovers and punchdowns. Aged in 27% new oak for 18 months. 13% alcohol. 510 cases made. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $143. click to buy.

2023 Hirsch Vineyards “San Andreas Fault” Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light to medium garnet in color, this wine smells of cranberry and cherry fruit with a hint of dried herbs and flowers. In the mouth, supple fine-grained tannins wrap around a silky core of cherries and raspberries shot through with crushed nuts, dried herbs and flowers, and a touch of oak. Lovely citrus peel and herb notes linger in the finish along with some toasted wood. Very pretty. Biodynamically grown fruit was destemmed, cold-soaked, and fermented in open-top fermenters with ambient yeasts, using a combination of pumpovers and punchdowns. Aged in 32% new oak for 22 months. 13% alcohol. 3061 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $84. click to buy.

2024 Hirsch Vineyards “The Bohan Dillon” Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light to medium garnet in color, this wine smells of cherries, redwood bark, and dried flowers. In the mouth, cherries, dried herbs, sawdust, and a touch of orange peel are wrapped in fine, gauzy tannins. Excellent acidity and length, with a touch of oak lingering in the finish. This is usually a wine made with fruit from both Hirsch and some of its neighbors on Bohan-Dillon Road, but this year the wine is made from all estate fruit. Destemmed, cold-soaked, and fermented in open-top fermenters with ambient yeasts, using a combination of pumpovers and punchdowns. Aged in 27% new oak for 9 months. 13% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $53. click to buy.

2023 Hirsch Vineyards “East Ridge” Pinot Noir, Fort Ross-Seaview, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of herbs, wet earth, raspberry, and cranberry fruit. In the mouth, cranberry and cherry fruit are wrapped in gauzy tannins and shot through with dried flowers and sweet oak notes. Supple and silky, with a nice stony quality underneath. Lovely acidity. This wine has a beautiful presence on the palate. Biodynamically grown fruit was destemmed, cold-soaked, and fermented in open-top fermenters with ambient yeasts, with a combination of pumpovers and punchdowns. Aged in 37% new oak for 18 months. 12.7% alcohol. 465 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $132. click to buy.

title: Introducing the Old Vine Registry Seal
summary:
I can’t tell you how many times I’ve picked up a bottle of wine that had the words “old vines,”

The post Introducing the Old Vine Registry Seal appeared first on Vinography.
content:
I can’t tell you how many times I’ve picked up a bottle of wine that had the words “old vines,” “vieilles vignes,” or “vigna vecchia” on the label and turned it around to find absolutely no further information about the vineyard that produced it. Were the vines 40 years old or 140? Did this come from one old vineyard or several? Those two words seem to be doing an awful lot of work while, at the same time, meaning almost nothing.

With the exception of a few regions in Spain (Priorat, Rioja, Ribera del Duero) and in Greece, the term “old vines” isn’t officially regulated or defined anywhere. Producers are free to use it however they like, regardless of actual vine age. And the reverse happens just as often: plenty of wines genuinely made from old vines never mention it at all, either because producers can’t be bothered, or because all of their vines are old and it doesn’t feel worth saying on every bottle.

That problem, multiplied by the hundreds of thousands around the world, is a big part of why the Old Vine Registry exists, and today I’m extremely proud to announce the next step in that project: the launch of the Old Vine Registry Seal. The OVR Seal is a program that allows producers, retailers, and importers to showcase wines made from the vineyards cataloged in the Old Vine Registry.

Wines made from old vines are special. They are different. They are less common. And consumers might appreciate that fact a bit more if they only had a way of consistently recognizing wines that were made from old vineyards around the world.

That’s what we’ve designed the OVR Seal to do. It clearly communicates that a wine comes from a registered vineyard, as well as the age category of that vineyard: 35+, 50+, 75+, 100+, and 150+ years old.

The seal, designed in several formats, is intended primarily for use on wine labels, but it can also appear on tech sheets, marketing materials, websites, e-commerce pages, and even vineyard signs, provided it remains associated with a specific registered vineyard, or a specific wine made from a registered vineyard.

It’s taken several months of hard work to pull this program together, with the help of stakeholders from several countries providing input into the early design drafts of the seal as well as the structure and terms of the program.

Meet the Launch Partners

The seal launches today with 11 initial launch partners—producers from 7 different countries—who were especially keen to be among the first to adopt the OVR Seal. They are:

  • AYA Estate – a beautiful Relais & Châteaux property in the Melnik region of Bulgaria with several plots of 51-year-old Cabernet Franc vines. Their 2024 Melnik, produced by Seewines Spirit and about to be released, will be the first commercially available bottle in the world bearing the OVR seal.
  • Bedrock Wine Co. – this Sonoma producer is one of the world’s premier stewards of old vineyards and a thought leader on old-vine wines and viticulture. Owner Morgan Twain-Peterson MW has written a very thoughtful article on why he is adopting the seal. Bedrock has a number of vineyards in the Old Vine Registry, including their eponymous Bedrock Vineyard, planted in 1888. The OVR Seal will appear on their 2026 wines, which will be released beginning in 2027.
  • Bodega Ciclo Andino – this boutique producer in Mendoza, Argentina, farms 18 acres of own-rooted Malbec vines planted in 1920. They will be using the OVR Seal on the soon-to-be-released 2024 vintage of their “Mas de Cien” Reserve Malbec.
  • Garage Wine Company – another globally recognized champion of old-vine wines and viticulture, founder Derek Mossman Knapp collaborates with farmers of several ancient vineyards in the Maule region of Chile, such as Nivaldo Morales and his 1900-planted Sauzal Vineyard. All of the Garage wines except those from Maipo will soon feature the OVR seal.
  • Methymnaeos Organic Vineyards – one of the pioneers of modern viticulture on the Greek island of Lesvos, Methymnaeos farms the oldest documented commercial planting on the island. Owner and winemaker Yannis Lambrou will use the OVR Seal on the upcoming releases of his 2023 and 2024 wines beginning in June of 2027.
  • Plaimont – this cooperative in the Gascony region of France has revitalized one of France’s oldest vineyards, the famous 1820-planted Pédebernarde vineyard, and farms many acres of old vineyards in Gascony and the Pyrenean foothills. Several of their wines will carry the OVR seal, but the first two to market will be their La Madeleine de Saint Mont and their Série XT Colombard Vieilles Vignes, both to be released in 2027.
  • Seghesio Family Vineyards – one of the most famous names in California Zinfandel, Seghesio farms several ancient vineyards, including their well-known Chianti Station vineyard planted in 1910. Seghesio will be using the OVR Seal on future bottlings of their Montafi Ranch Red Blend, Seghesio Home Ranch Zinfandel, and Chianti Station Sangiovese Blend.
  • Sown Estate – a newer, family-run property in Napa, Sown Estate farms a spectacular 35-year-old hillside vineyard at 1,100 feet of elevation on the slopes of Mount George in Napa above the Coombsville AVA. Their estate wines will feature the OVR Seal when they are next labeled and bottled.
  • Tenuta Santa Maria di Gaetano Bertani – The Bertani family has been making wine in the Veneto region since at least 1567. Among their many vineyard holdings is the 1965-planted Lepiga Vineyard. Tenuta Santa Maria will be featuring the OVR Seal on their 2026 Lepiga Soave, which will be released in 2027.
  • Versado Wine – This tiny producer in the Lujan de Cuyo region of Mendoza in Argentina farms 7.4 acres of own-rooted Malbec planted in 1920. Their 2020 Centenary Vines Malbec, to be released in March of 2027, will carry the OVR Seal.
  • Wooldridge Creek Winery – located in Oregon’s Applegate Valley, this family-run estate farms a large vineyard site planted in the late 1970s and early 1980s. They produce an array of wines that will soon bear the OVR Seal.

Why This Matters

The Old Vine Registry’s mission has three pillars: Identify, Value, and Preserve. The registry exists first to identify and catalog old vineyards around the world for the simple reason that you can’t preserve what you don’t know about. Secondly, the stories of these vineyards, the people who farm them, and the wines they make need to be documented and told. Only then will people understand the value of these vineyards and be willing to pay for the wines they produce. If we can get people to buy the wines, then the vineyards will continue to have economic value for those who farm them, and we can begin the conversation around preserving them. We don’t preserve what we don’t value.

As the largest and most authoritative database of 35+ year-old vineyards around the world, the Old Vine Registry has made great progress on the identification piece of that mission. We’ve come a long way from an 1800-line spreadsheet in just three years, but there’s plenty more work ahead. The OVR Seal represents the next step towards fulfilling that mission. By giving wine producers, importers, and retailers the ability to clearly identify wines made from registered vineyards, we’re hoping to move the old-vine conversation down to the level of the shelf or the wine list, where it actually reaches wine drinkers.

The hope is that the OVR Seal can play a part in helping to create a viable commercial category for old-vine wines. It’s not hard to imagine a day when you could walk into a wine shop and find a section dedicated to old-vine wines, or filter an e-commerce site for them. Restaurants could carve out a section of their wine list, or just put an icon next to old-vine bottles. Importers could let buyers sort and filter their portfolios the same way. When such options become a reality, we will have moved the conversation about old vines and their value to center stage, where it belongs.

If you happen to be a wine producer with a qualifying vineyard, you can submit your vineyard to the Old Vine Registry for free, and once it’s in the database, you can register to use the OVR seal.

If you’re a wine lover, the easiest place to start engaging with old vineyards is to pull an old-vine bottle off the shelf and see whether it’s already in the Registry. If it’s not, you can submit it yourself, or reach out to the producer and encourage them to do so.

So the next time one of us turns around a bottle looking for an answer, we can find one.

summary:
